text: Build 5, and this time the idea came from CH talking it through with the other robot thread: something that feels alive, a whole world, hands-off. The plan they agreed: an island that is always running. No server. The page works out the island from the real clock, so everyone who opens it sees the same island at the same moment.

The rule that makes it last: every new rule gets a start date. Rain, predators, seasons, whatever comes later, each one only exists from the day it's added. So the island's past never changes, and a test pins it down. Shift 1 is small on purpose: bare island, real day and night, grass that spreads, and one grazing animal that eats, breeds and can starve.

Two things I'll hold you to. The past: a pinned fingerprint of the island on an early day, and a check that a rule dated in the future changes nothing before its date. And honesty about the start: if the island 'began' a week ago, the page says it was worked out backwards from the rules, not that it ran on a server all week.
Agreed. The island rose on October 26, 2026, midnight island time, which is UTC minus 5 all year. That gives it a week of history today. The grazers arrive on day 2.

Here's the plan. 1) The clock: island time, ten-minute ticks, and the real sun's height for the island's spot. 2) The island: a fixed shape of sand, soil and rock. 3) Grass: grows in daylight, spreads tile to tile. 4) Grazers: arrive on day 2, eat, wander to greener ground, sleep at night, breed when fed, starve when not. 5) History lines: the island writes down what happened, day by day. 6) The past pinned: a fingerprint test, and a rule-start-date test. 7) The page: watch it live, replay the last 24 hours, read its history. One step at a time, a test with each, and the skeptic checks every one.

text: Step 1: the clock. Tick 0 is midnight, October 26, island time; ten minutes a tick. The sun is the real one for a spot at 18.5 degrees north on New York's longitude: today it rises about 6:04 am and sets about 5:23 pm. Tested against the seasons: noon sun about 48 degrees high on the December solstice and 85 in June, as the textbook sums say for that latitude.

text: Step 2: the island. One fixed shape from a fixed seed, so it's the same for everyone forever: a beach all the way round, soil inside, and a ring of rocky outcrops on the high ground. The first try was a round blob with a solid slab of rock in the middle, so I gave the coast more bite and made the rock come in ridges. Tested: one island with no stray islets, sea all round the map edge, sand exactly where land meets sea, and only soil can grow things.

text: Steps 3, 4 and 5 in one, because the history lines come from the rules themselves. Grass grows in daylight and spreads tile to tile from one seed that lands on the south beach at first light. Two grazers wash ashore on day 2 at 8 am; they eat lush grass, step toward greener ground, sleep at night, have young when well fed, starve when not, and if they all die, two more try ten days later. Every rule rolls its own dice per tick, so a rule added later can't nudge another. Tuning took four tries: the first herds hit the 600 cap and sat there, eating the island brown, or starved by the hundred every single day. Now they leave the roots to grow back, and only record-breaking hunger makes the history.

text: Step 6: the past, pinned. A fingerprint of the whole island (every blade of grass to four decimals, every grazer, every history line) at noon on days 3, 5 and 7, written into a test. And a made-up 'blight' rule that kills all the grass, plugged in with a start on day 9: before day 9 the island is identical to the last digit, after it isn't. That's the promise for every future shift, as a test.
subject: Pin the island's past: fingerprints, and a later rule can't touch it

text: Step 7: the page. Open it and your browser works the island out to this very minute, then moves it on every ten minutes. Grazers hop between tiles, sleep with their eyes shut at night, and the sea gets stars after dusk. Hover one to meet it. A button replays the last 24 hours in about 13 seconds, night and all. Below: everything that happened, and every rule with the time it began. Tested in a headless browser with its clock frozen at noon today: it shows Day 7, the same grazer count and history the rules give for that moment, and the replay passes through last night.
subject: The page: the island live, a 24-hour replay, its history and its rules

text: Opened it at noon on day 7 (screenshots from the browser test). What I saw: a blue sea with a slow shimmer, the south half of the island green, 13 grazers dotted over it, the north half still bare brown soil because the grass started from one seed on the south beach and hasn't got there yet. Pressed replay: the sky goes orange at dusk, then dark blue with stars, the grazers close their eyes and stop. It feels like a place.

Two honest gripes. It's slow on purpose, so if you open it once you see a still picture; the replay button is what sells it. And grazers are one tile wide, so you have to aim to hover one. Writing both down for shift 2 instead of fiddling now.
Wrote down what's on the island, the promise that its past never changes and how the tests hold us to it, how to run it, and what isn't tested, including the playtester's two gripes.

Shift 1 over. 7 commits, 28 tests. The skeptic believed every logic commit this time; the hard part was tuning, which no test can judge, so the playtester looked. The island is on day 7 with its grazers still multiplying. Shift 2 ideas from the playtester's notes: something you see the moment you open it, and grazers you can actually point at. Then rain, seasons, a predator, each starting on the day it's added.
